course.title: Medical Spanish for Healthcare
course.description: A CEFR B1-level Spanish-for-specific-purposes course for healthcare workers, building the vocabulary and phrasing needed to greet patients, take histories, explain procedures, and handle emergencies in Latin-American Spanish.

lessons.title: Greeting patients & taking a history
lessons.grammar_note: Address adult patients with the polite usted form: use está (not estás) and su (not tu). It signals respect and is the default in every clinical setting.

items.example: Buenos días, soy la doctora Ramírez. ¿Cómo se siente hoy?
Cuénteme, ¿qué lo trae por aquí hoy?
Voy a preguntarle por sus antecedentes médicos.

lessons.title: Body parts & symptoms
lessons.grammar_note: Spanish uses the definite article, not a possessive, with body parts: me duele la cabeza (my head hurts), never me duele mi cabeza.

items.example: Me duele la cabeza desde ayer.
Le duele el estómago después de comer.
Cuando me paro rápido siento mareo.
Tengo tos seca hace tres días.

lessons.title: Giving instructions: usted commands
lessons.grammar_note: Form usted commands from the yo present tense: drop the -o and add the opposite vowel — hablo → hable, como → coma, respiro → respire.

sections.heading: Building the command
sections.text: For instructions to a patient you use the usted command. Take the yo form of the present tense, drop the final -o, and add -e for -ar verbs or -a for -er/-ir verbs: respirar → respiro → respire (breathe), abrir → abro → abra (open). So respire hondo means take a deep breath and abra la boca means open your mouth.

sections.heading: Negative commands
sections.text: To tell someone not to do something, place no before the same form: no coma nada antes del examen (do not eat anything before the exam), no se levante todavía (do not get up yet). The form never changes; you only add no in front.

sections.heading: Pronouns with commands
sections.text: In an affirmative command, object and reflexive pronouns attach to the end: siéntese (sit down), quítese la camisa (take off your shirt), respírelo lento. In a negative command they go before the verb: no se mueva (do not move), no lo tome con el estómago vacío.

sections.heading: Common irregulars
sections.text: A few high-frequency verbs are irregular: ir → vaya (go), dar → dé, estar → esté, ser → sea. Useful in the clinic: vaya al laboratorio (go to the lab) and esté tranquilo (stay calm).

body.scenario: A clinic in Guadalajara. A new patient arrives with a two-day headache. Greet them, ask what brings them in, ask since when and how strong the pain is, and ask about medications and allergies before moving on.
body.persona: A polite 58-year-old patient who answers briefly and expects to be addressed with usted; speaks no English
body.goal: Complete a basic history — chief complaint, timeline, medications, and allergies — entirely in Spanish

lessons.title: At the pharmacy: medications
lessons.grammar_note: Dosage frequency uses cada + time: cada ocho horas (every eight hours). Cada is invariable — it never changes for gender or number.

items.example: Tome una pastilla con el desayuno.
El jarabe es para la tos.
Aquí tiene la receta para la farmacia.
Tome el antibiótico cada ocho horas.
Esta pastilla se toma en ayunas.
Puede tener sueño; es uno de los efectos secundarios.

lessons.title: The subjunctive for advice
lessons.grammar_note: After le recomiendo que and es importante que, the second verb goes in the subjunctive: le recomiendo que descanse (I recommend that you rest).

sections.heading: Why the subjunctive here
sections.text: When you advise or recommend rather than state a fact, Spanish switches to the subjunctive in the second clause. The trigger is a phrase of recommendation plus que: le recomiendo que…, le sugiero que…, es importante que…, es mejor que…. The advice verb stays normal; the verb after que becomes subjunctive.

sections.heading: Forming the present subjunctive
sections.text: It is built exactly like the usted command, then given full endings. From tomar: tome, tomes, tome, tomemos, tomen. From beber: beba, bebas, beba, bebamos, beban. So le recomiendo que tome mucha agua (I recommend you drink plenty of water) and es importante que beba líquidos (it is important that you drink fluids).

sections.heading: Softening advice
sections.text: The subjunctive makes advice sound caring rather than commanding. Compare the blunt command tome agua (drink water) with le recomiendo que tome agua (I recommend you drink water). In sensitive conversations the recommendation form feels more respectful and less like an order.

sections.heading: Key irregular verbs
sections.text: Learn a few irregulars that come up constantly in advice: ir → vaya (es importante que vaya al hospital), hacer → haga (le sugiero que haga reposo), ser → sea, and estar → esté (es mejor que esté tranquilo).

body.scenario: An emergency department in Lima. A patient reports abdominal pain. Ask them to rate the pain from 0 to 10, ask where exactly it hurts, whether it is sharp or dull and whether it comes and goes, and what makes it better or worse.
body.persona: A worried 34-year-old patient in real discomfort who describes symptoms vividly and needs reassurance
body.goal: Characterize the pain — intensity, location, quality, and pattern — using a 0-to-10 scale in Spanish

lessons.title: Writing discharge instructions
lessons.grammar_note: Written instructions mix usted commands (tome, aplique) with recommendation phrases (se recomienda que…) — keep the register polite and clear.

sections.heading: Purpose and tone
sections.text: Discharge instructions (las indicaciones de alta) tell the patient what to do at home in plain, respectful Spanish. Write short numbered steps, use usted commands for actions, and avoid technical jargon. Start with a one-line summary: Le explicamos cómo cuidarse en casa después de su visita.

sections.heading: Medication section
sections.text: State each medicine, its dose, and its timing clearly: Tome un comprimido de paracetamol cada ocho horas si tiene dolor o fiebre. Termine todo el antibiótico aunque se sienta mejor. Add cautions where needed: No tome este medicamento con el estómago vacío.

sections.heading: Activity and follow-up
sections.text: Explain rest, diet, and the next appointment: Se recomienda que descanse hoy y mañana y que beba abundantes líquidos. Regrese a control en cinco días o antes si no mejora. Naming the timeframe prevents confusion about when to come back.

sections.heading: Warning signs
sections.text: Close with clear red flags and what to do: Vuelva a urgencias de inmediato si tiene fiebre alta, dificultad para respirar o dolor en el pecho. A short warning-signs list at the end is the most important part of any discharge note.

body.scenario: An ambulance bay in Bogotá. A patient arrives short of breath after a fall. Keep them calm, give clear usted commands (breathe slowly, do not move, look at me), ask quick yes/no questions about pain and allergies, and explain the next step before you act.
body.persona: A frightened, breathless patient who can only give short answers and needs firm, calm direction
body.goal: Stabilize communication in a crisis — reassure, instruct, and gather critical information fast in Spanish

questions.prompt: How do you tell a patient to take a deep breath (usted command)?
questions.explanation: The usted command of respirar is respire: respiro → drop the -o → add -e. Respire hondo means take a deep breath.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly says "my head hurts"?
questions.explanation: With body parts Spanish uses the definite article, not a possessive: me duele la cabeza.

questions.prompt: "Cada ocho horas" on a prescription means…
questions.explanation: Cada + a time span means every: cada ocho horas is every eight hours.

questions.prompt: Complete the advice: "Le recomiendo que ___ mucha agua."
questions.explanation: After le recomiendo que the verb is subjunctive: tome. The command-like form carries the recommendation.

questions.prompt: A patient says "en ayunas." You should take the medicine…
questions.explanation: En ayunas means on an empty stomach, typically before eating in the morning.

questions.prompt: Which is the polite, respectful way to greet an adult patient?
questions.explanation: The usted form ¿cómo se siente? is the respectful clinical default; the tú forms are too informal for a new patient.
